hook: A service could prevent expensive illnesses, yet none of the people who save money can fund it.
readerPromise: Identify institutional reasons a worthwhile technical possibility may never find a sponsor.
protectedRevelations: Specific financing prescriptions and final reform proposals
visualPlan: Possible, yet missing: Place prevention costs in one budget and future savings in several other budgets with no paying owner. Hold the useful project between those budgets, showing the missing sponsor rather than a broken invention.

Who would pay for success?: Follow one prevented cost toward the beneficiary while the developer's funding line remains empty. Show an open tool used by several participants without assigning exclusive ownership to one.

The barriers between institutions: Place the same proposal before investor, public funder and professional authority with distinct unanswered conditions. Name Missing sponsor beside the proposal, without suggesting every refusal has the same cause.
Investigate the absent future: Keep the feasible project on the workbench while the room for a sponsor remains empty. End on the project and its unanswered funding question, not a triumphant launch.

cueChanges.nextVisualChange: Keep the workable prototype separate from the empty institutional place meant to receive it.
Use one benefit crossing a budget boundary; avoid a catalogue of fifteen patterns on screen.
Preserve distinct funding and authority boundaries with one clear action each.
Close on the opening diagnostic page and the unresolved sponsor position.

independentReview.notes: Every spoken sentence reviewed against canonical English short reader for clear newcomer meaning, source grounding, curiosity and emotional intent. sentenceIntentions.text: A service could prevent expensive illnesses, yet none of the people who save money can fund it.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Show the preventive-service funding mismatch concretely
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Recognize useful projects that no benefiting budget can sponsor

sentenceIntentions.text: Artificial Impossibility names this gap: a useful project with no workable place in existing institutions.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Name artificial impossibility as an institutional gap
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Understand the distinctive concept without assuming technology has failed

sentenceIntentions.text: A preventive service may save money for someone who never pays its developer.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Show preventive value crossing a payer's boundary

sentenceIntentions.text: An open tool may create value precisely because nobody can own the whole advantage.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Explain why openness can undermine exclusive ownership

sentenceIntentions.text: The book follows these gaps through investment, public funding, professional power, and services people share.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Locate recurring barriers across funding and authority

sentenceIntentions.text: Its named patterns help explain why resistance to change is sometimes the wrong diagnosis.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Offer precise patterns instead of vague resistance stories
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Become curious about named mechanisms behind absence

sentenceIntentions.text: A missing invention starts to look like a question about who could afford to make it possible.
sentenceIntentions.purpose: Make unseen projects relevant to founders and citizens
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Notice that missing innovations can carry evidence

sentenceIntentions.text: Begin with the missing sponsor, and consider which possible futures never reach a demonstration.
sentenceIntentions.viewerResponse: Wonder which feasible futures lack an institutional home

distinctiveContribution: Artificial impossibility names technically plausible projects whose value does not fit ordinary sponsorship, ownership or funding mandates.
